seo.shortDescription: Searchable 2026 U.S. tariff table for all 118 HTS Chapter 95 lines — toys, dolls, puzzles, video game consoles, board games, Christmas decorations, golf clubs, exercise equipment, fishing tackle. Base rates Free to 9.2%, plus the extra duty by country: China and Vietnam +12.5%, EU 10% in total, Canada 50% on toys and consoles.

overview.intro:
Chapter 95 covers toys, dolls and puzzles (heading 9503), video game consoles, card, board and arcade games (9504), Christmas and other festive articles (9505), sports and exercise equipment (9506), fishing tackle (9507) and amusement park rides (9508). The base rates are among the **lowest in the tariff schedule**: 70 of the 118 lines are **Free**, including every toy, game console, playing card, Christmas decoration and amusement ride. The 48 dutiable lines are sports goods and fishing tackle, at 2.6% to 9.2% (fishing reels between $2.70 and $8.45: 24¢ each).

The U.S. imported **$37.02B** of Chapter 95 goods in 2025, 14.7% less than in 2024. **China** still supplied $20.19B (54.5%), but that was down 37.0% in a year; **Vietnam** more than doubled to $7.13B, ahead of Mexico ($1.96B), Taiwan ($1.33B) and Japan ($873M). Toys (9503) were $14.68B and video game consoles (9504.50) $6.73B.

So the duty a shipment pays is mostly the **extra duty by country**. Since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 tariff on 60 economies adds **+12.5% for China, Vietnam and Thailand** and **+10% for Indonesia, Cambodia, India and Malaysia**; **EU goods pay 10% in total** and **Japanese 12.5% in total**, so a Free toy from Germany or Japan now pays 10% or 12.5%. China adds **+7.5% (List 4A)** on 81 lines, mostly sports goods — but **toys, video game consoles, playing cards, board games and most Christmas decorations were on List 4B, which was suspended**, so Chinese toys and consoles pay 12.5%. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico pay nothing; from **Canada, toys, video game consoles, arcade games, hockey equipment, exercise equipment, pools and other listed goods — 27 lines — pay a 50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA**.

productGroups.label: Toys, dolls, puzzles, building sets, scale models, tricycles and toy scooters
productGroups.blurb: Toys of every kind — dolls and plush toys, building blocks and construction sets, puzzles, ride-on toys (tricycles, toy scooters, pedal cars), toy balls and balloons, scale models and hobby kits — and their parts. One 8-digit line, 9503.00.00, Free; the statistical suffix says whether it is an inflatable ball or balloon or another toy, and the youngest age it is labeled for (under 3, 3 to 12, or not a children's product). The extra duty by origin is what costs: 12.5% from China or Vietnam, 10% from the EU, 50% from Canada even under USMCA.

productGroups.label: Video game consoles, board and card games, billiards, arcade, casino and bowling equipment
productGroups.blurb: Video game consoles and handheld game machines with their controllers and parts (9504.50), coin- or card-operated arcade and pinball machines (9504.30), playing and trading cards (9504.40), chess, checkers, darts, dice, poker chips and other board games (9504.90.60), billiard tables and balls, bowling balls and equipment. Every line is Free; the extra duty depends on the country.

productGroups.label: Christmas ornaments, artificial Christmas trees, Halloween and party articles, magic tricks
productGroups.blurb: Christmas ornaments (of glass, wood or other materials), nativity scenes, artificial Christmas trees, wreaths and other Christmas decorations, Halloween and other holiday decorations, party favors, confetti and noisemakers, magic tricks and practical jokes. All Free. Christmas lighting strings are heading 9405, and utilitarian holiday articles (tableware, linens) are classified by material.

productGroups.label: Sports and exercise equipment: golf, balls, skis, skates, fitness machines, pools, archery, hockey
productGroups.blurb: Sports and fitness equipment. Free: golf balls, soccer balls and footballs, baseballs, tennis balls, ski and snowboard parts, water skis and surfboards, roller skates, archery, hockey and lacrosse gear. Dutiable 2.6%–5.6%: golf clubs 4.4%, golf parts 4.9%, basketballs and volleyballs 4.8%, tennis rackets 5.3%, table tennis 5.1%, treadmills, exercise bikes and other fitness equipment 4.6%, swimming pools 5.3%, other sports goods 4%.

productGroups.label: Fishing rods, reels, hooks, line, lures and other fishing tackle; landing nets
productGroups.blurb: Fishing tackle — every line is dutiable: rods 6%, hooks 4%–4.8%, reels 9.2% (up to $2.70 each), 24¢ each ($2.70–$8.45) or 3.9% (over $8.45), reel parts 5.4%, retail fishing line 3.7%, leaders 5.6%, landing and butterfly nets 5%, artificial baits and flies 9%, other tackle 9%. A separate federal excise tax of 10% (rods capped at $10) applies when the importer sells them.

productGroups.label: Amusement park rides, carousels, water park and fairground amusements, traveling circuses and theaters
productGroups.blurb: Roller coasters, carousels and swings, bumper cars, motion simulators, water rides and water park amusements, fairground games, traveling circuses and theaters. All Free; home and playground equipment is not included.

workedExamples.title: Toys from China — Free base rate, 12.5% in total
workedExamples.body: Toys labeled for ages 3 to 12 are Free. China pays the 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.31): **12.5%**, $1,250 on a $10,000 shipment. Toys were moved to List 4B, which USTR suspended in December 2019, so no List 4A duty is added. In April–May 2025 the same shipment paid 145% (125% reciprocal + 20% fentanyl IEEPA duties), and 20% from November 10, 2025 until the IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026.

workedExamples.title: Video game consoles: China, Vietnam, Japan, Canada
workedExamples.body: Consoles, handheld game machines and their controllers are Free. From China or Vietnam they pay **12.5%** (9903.05.31, 9903.05.84; consoles were on suspended List 4B), from Japan 12.5% in total (9903.05.49), from Malaysia or Indonesia 10%. From Canada 9504.50 is on the Section 338 list (9903.03.14): **50% even with a USMCA claim**, 60% without one.

workedExamples.title: Golf clubs from China, Vietnam or Japan
workedExamples.body: Complete golf clubs pay 4.4%. 9506.31 is on China's List 4A, so Chinese clubs pay 4.4% + 12.5% + 7.5% = **24.4%** — $2,440 on $10,000. Vietnamese clubs pay 16.9%, Taiwanese 10% in total (9903.05.76), Japanese 12.5% in total even though the U.S.–Japan Trade Agreement (JP) removes the 4.4% (U.S. note 52(a) charges the Section 301 duty on FTA goods too). Golf balls (9506.32) are Free: 20% from China.

workedExamples.title: Treadmills and exercise bikes from China or Taiwan
workedExamples.body: Exercise equipment pays 4.6%. From China it is a List 4A line: 4.6% + 12.5% + 7.5% = **24.6%**. From Taiwan 10% in total, from Vietnam 17.1%. From August 18, 2025 to April 5, 2026 the steel content of exercise equipment also paid the 50% Section 232 duty (and the aluminum content from March 12, 2025); Proclamation 11021 left 9506.91 off the new metals lists. From Canada, 9506.91 owes the 50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA.

workedExamples.title: Artificial Christmas trees and ornaments from China
workedExamples.body: Artificial Christmas trees of plastics are Free and pay **12.5%** from China — 9505.10.40 was on the suspended List 4B. Glass ornaments (9505.10.10) are on List 4A: 20%. Christmas light sets are not in this chapter (heading 9405). Christmas tableware and other utilitarian articles shaped like a holiday symbol can enter Free under 9817.95.05, a Chapter 98 provision the 2026 Section 301 duty does not reach.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** This chapter does not cover: (a) candles (3406); (b) fireworks (3604); (c) fishing yarns, monofilament, cords or gut cut to length but not made up into fishing lines; (d) sports bags (4202, 4303, 4304); (e) fancy dress and sports clothing of textiles (chapters 61, 62); (f) textile flags or sails (chapter 63); (g) sports footwear (other than skating boots with skates attached) of chapter 64 or sports headgear of chapter 65; (h) walking-sticks, whips and riding-crops (6602, 6603); (ij) unmounted glass eyes for dolls (7018); (k) parts of general use of base metal or plastics; (l) bells and gongs (8306); (m) pumps, filters, electric motors, transformers, recording media, radio remote controls and infrared remote controls; (n) sports vehicles other than sleds and toboggans (section XVII); (o) children's bicycles (8712); (p) unmanned aircraft — drones (8806); (q) canoes, skiffs and other sports craft (chapter 89); (r) sports goggles (9004); (s) decoy calls or whistles (9208); (t) arms of chapter 93; (u) lighting strings of all kinds (9405); (v) monopods, bipods and tripods (9620); (w) racket strings, tents and camping goods, gloves and mitts (by material); or (x) tableware, kitchenware, toilet articles, carpets, apparel, bed, table, toilet and kitchen linen and similar utilitarian articles (by material; see 9817.95.01 and 9817.95.05).

**Note 2.** The chapter includes articles in which pearls, precious or semiprecious stones or precious metal are only minor constituents.

**Note 3.** Parts and accessories suitable for use solely or principally with articles of this chapter are classified with those articles.

**Note 4.** Heading 9503 covers toys combined with other items that are not sets under General Interpretative Rule 3(b), when put up together for retail sale and the combination has the essential character of a toy.

**Note 5.** Heading 9503 does not cover articles identifiable as intended exclusively for animals — pet toys are classified in their own heading.

**Note 6.** For heading 9508: "amusement park rides" carry or direct persons over or through a fixed or restricted course or within a defined area for amusement, and do not include equipment of a kind commonly installed in residences or playgrounds; "water park amusements" are equipment designed specifically for water parks; "fairground amusements" are games of chance, strength or skill commonly run by an operator, other than equipment of heading 9504.

**Subheading note 1.** Subheading 9504.50 covers video game consoles from which the image is reproduced on a television receiver, a monitor or another external screen or surface, and video game machines with a self-contained screen, portable or not; coin-, banknote-, card- or token-operated machines go to 9504.30.

**Statistical note 1.** In heading 9503, classification follows the youngest age for which the product is intended — an item labeled "For ages 2–5" goes in the "Under 3 years of age" category. Parts and accessories not labeled for an age follow the finished retail product they belong to.

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 95: Toys, Games & Sports Equipment — Tariff Updates

seo.title: Toy Tariffs 2026: HTS Chapter 95 Tariff Updates Since January 2025 — China, Vietnam, Canada, Video Game Consoles | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for U.S. tariffs on toys, video game consoles, Christmas decorations and sporting goods since January 2025: the IEEPA duties (up to 145% on Chinese toys) and their end, Section 122, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs, China List 4A and 4B, Canada's 50% Section 338 duty, Section 232 metals and the CPSC eFiling rule, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). **No Chapter 95 base rate changed**: all 118 lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates — Free on toys, consoles, games, Christmas articles and rides, 2.6% to 9.2% on sports goods and fishing tackle.

Everything that changed sits on top of the base rate. In 2025 the IEEPA duties reached toys from every country: **Chinese toys paid 145% in April–May 2025**, then 30% and from November 10, 2025 20%; Vietnam 20%, Indonesia, Cambodia, Thailand and Malaysia 19%, the EU 15% in total. The IEEPA duties **ended on February 24, 2026** (importers can claim refunds through CBP's CAPE process), and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026** goods from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff**: +12.5% for China, Vietnam and Thailand, +10% for Indonesia, Cambodia, India and Malaysia, 10% in total for the EU and 12.5% in total for Japan. China still pays **+7.5% (List 4A)** on 81 lines, mostly sports goods; toys and consoles were on List 4B, which stays suspended. Since **August 22, 2026** Canadian toys, consoles, hockey equipment and other goods on 27 lines pay a **50% Section 338 duty**, even under USMCA. The Section 232 metals duties that reached exercise equipment, fishing reels and other sports goods in 2025 ended April 6, 2026, except for Russian aluminum. And since **July 8, 2026** importers of toys and other children's products must **eFile** their Children's Product Certificate data with the entry.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 95 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the China Section 301 List 4A duty (and the suspended List 4B), the Canada Section 338 duty, Russia's rates in lieu of column 2 and the 200% Section 232 duty on Russian aluminum, the Nicaragua Section 301 duty scheduled for 2027, the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties and Section 232 metals duties that have ended, and the suspension of de minimis. CPSC toy-safety and certificate rules are listed with their effective dates. No antidumping or countervailing duty order covers a Chapter 95 product, and no Section 232 action other than the Russian aluminum duty reaches Chapter 95 today. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

inEffect.now: +20% on 81 lines; +12.5% on the 37 former List 4B lines (toys, consoles, games)

The other 37 lines — 28 subheadings including **toys (9503), video game consoles (9504.50), playing cards, board games, billiard tables, Christmas decorations other than glass ornaments, artificial Christmas trees, festive articles**, table tennis, tennis and badminton rackets, roller skates, baseball equipment, fishing rods, cheaper reels and nets — were put on List 4B (9903.88.16), which USTR suspended before it took effect, so they pay only +12.5%. changes.title: No Chapter 95 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 118 Chapter 95 lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition, and no line was added, split or renumbered.

changes.title: CBP proposes new entry rules for low-value and mail shipments
changes.detail: CBP proposed to change filing requirements for informal entries of goods valued at $2,500 or less, create an electronic informal entry type for mail and add bonding requirements. Comments are due December 7, 2026. It would change how small parcels of toys are entered, not their duty rate.

changes.title: China Section 301 List 4A continues after the four-year review
changes.detail: USTR announced that the China Section 301 actions did not terminate on their anniversaries because domestic industries asked for them to continue. For Chapter 95 this keeps +7.5% (List 4A, 9903.88.15) on 81 lines; List 4B, with toys and consoles, stays suspended.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 list revised: fishing-rod parts removed
changes.detail: Proclamation 11065 (Annex I, Part B) took fishing-rod parts and accessories (9507.10.00.80) off the motor-vehicle list from September 15, 2026; fishing rods themselves (9507.10.00.40) stay at 50%. Proclamations 11064 and 11065 added no Chapter 95 provision, and from this date the duty also applies on top of any Section 232 duty.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 duty: 50% on Canadian toys, consoles, hockey sticks and sports goods
changes.detail: Proclamations 11046 and 11048 (July 20, 2026) imposed a 50% duty on listed products of Canada after Proclamation 11056 moved the start from August 19 to August 22, 2026. In Chapter 95 it reached 28 lines: toys (all of 9503.00.00), coin-operated and arcade games (9504.30), video game consoles and controllers (9504.50), other game machines (9504.90.40), Christmas ornaments other than glass or wood (9505.10.25), Halloween and other festive articles (9505.90.60), golf club parts and other golf equipment (9506.39), ice skates (9506.70.40, 9506.70.60), exercise equipment (9506.91), swimming pools (9506.99.55), other sports goods (9506.99.60) and fishing rods (9507.10.00.40) on the motor-vehicle list (9903.03.14), and ice- and field-hockey equipment (9506.99.25) on the alcoholic-beverage list (9903.03.12), and fishing-rod parts and accessories (9507.10.00.80) until September 14. Unlike the Section 301 duty, it applies to USMCA-qualifying goods too (U.S. note 51(a)).

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies cover all of Chapter 95
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84). No Chapter 95 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)) or on any country exception list (note 52(j)). China, Vietnam, Thailand and the Philippines +12.5%; Indonesia, Cambodia, India and Malaysia +10%. EU goods pay 10% in total and Japanese and Korean 12.5% in total — on Free toys and games that is the whole rate. FTA goods pay it too (note 52(a)). USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94).

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil
changes.detail: 25% on all goods of Brazil (9903.05.01). No Chapter 95 line is on the Brazil exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii)). From July 24 the 12.5% forced-labor tariff (9903.05.27) is added on top.

changes.title: CPSC eFiling: certificate data must be filed with the entry
changes.detail: CPSC's revised certificates rule (16 CFR part 1110) took effect: importers of toys and other products that need a Children's Product Certificate or General Certificate of Conformity must eFile the certificate data elements in ACE when they file the entry (for mail shipments, in CPSC's Product Registry before arrival). Goods entered from a foreign-trade zone follow from January 8, 2027. It adds no duty.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still remove the Section 301 duty on Mexican and Canadian goods — but not the Section 338 duty on the 27 listed Canadian lines.

changes.title: CPSC keeps the lead limits for toys and children's products
changes.detail: CPSC's periodic review found that the current limits — 100 ppm lead in any accessible component of a children's product and 90 ppm (0.009%) lead in paint and surface coatings — are already the lowest technologically feasible, so it did not change them.

changes.title: CBP suspends de minimis indefinitely
changes.detail: Two interim final rules suspend the $800 de minimis exemption in CBP's regulations: 19 CFR 10.151(b) for every mode except mail, and 19 CFR 145.31(b) for mail, until CBP announces otherwise. A toy shipped direct to a U.S. consumer needs an entry and pays the full duty — base rate plus the extra duty for its origin. The new postal informal entry process took effect July 24, 2026.

changes.title: CPSC toy standard adds neck-float requirements
changes.detail: A new 16 CFR 1250.5 sets performance and labeling requirements for baby neck floats under the toy standard. Third-party testing and certification was extended to August 16, 2026 for importers that submitted a sample to CPSC.

changes.title: CBP opens CAPE for IEEPA duty refunds
changes.detail: CBP deployed the Consolidated Administration and Processing of Entries (CAPE) function in ACE: importers of record and their brokers file a CAPE Declaration listing entries, and ACE removes the IEEPA Chapter 99 lines and refunds the IEEPA duties with interest, generally within 60–90 days. Phase 1 covers unliquidated entries and entries still within the voluntary reliquidation period. The Section 301, List 4A and Section 338 duties are not refunded.

changes.title: Section 232 metals duties on sports goods end (except Russia)
changes.detail: Proclamation 11021 replaced the Section 232 aluminum and steel derivative headings with new 9903.82 headings and new product lists (U.S. note 16(c)). No Chapter 95 line is on them, so exercise equipment, fishing reels, pools and the other derivative lines no longer pay a metals duty. The 200% duty on Russian aluminum (9903.85.68) still applies to the 22 lines.

changes.title: CPSC toy standard adds water-bead requirements
changes.detail: A new 16 CFR 1250.4 sets performance and labeling requirements for water bead toys and toys containing water beads, in addition to ASTM F963-23.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. No Chapter 95 subheading was on the product exemption lists (9903.03.03–9903.03.06). USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil, India and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: De minimis suspension continued after the IEEPA ruling
changes.detail: Executive Order 14388 kept duty-free de minimis treatment suspended for all countries.

changes.title: India's extra 25% IEEPA duty removed
changes.detail: Executive Order 14384 ended the additional 25% duty on products of India (9903.01.84) from February 7, 2026. The 25% reciprocal rate on India ended with the other IEEPA duties on February 24.

changes.title: AGOA reauthorized through December 31, 2026
changes.detail: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75) renewed AGOA retroactively from September 30, 2025. AGOA (SPI D) makes the dutiable sports and fishing lines of Chapter 95 Free for eligible sub-Saharan countries; toys and games are Free for everyone. GSP (SPI A) remains expired since December 31, 2020.

changes.title: Scheduled: Section 301 tariff on products of Nicaragua
changes.detail: USTR's implementation notice: products of Nicaragua that pay the column 1-general rate (that is, not entered under CAFTA-DR) will pay +10% (9903.89.01) from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028, on every Chapter 95 line. Today Nicaragua pays the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.58).

changes.title: China fentanyl duty cut to 10%
changes.detail: The IEEPA duty on products of China and Hong Kong (9903.01.24) fell from +20% to +10%, so Chinese toys and consoles paid 20% (10% + 10% reciprocal) until February 23, 2026.

changes.title: De minimis exemption suspended for all countries
changes.detail: Executive Order 14324 ended duty-free entry for shipments valued at $800 or less from every country, effective for goods entered from August 29, 2025. Toys ordered online from overseas sellers have paid duty since then.

changes.title: Extra 25% on products of India
changes.detail: Executive Order 14329 added 25% on Indian goods (9903.01.84), on top of the 25% reciprocal rate in force since August 7, 2025 (EO 14326): 50% in all on Indian toys and sports goods. Ended February 7, 2026.

changes.title: Exercise equipment added to the Section 232 steel derivative list
changes.detail: Commerce's first inclusions round added 9506.91.00 (exercise cycles, rowing machines and other fitness equipment) to the steel derivative list of U.S. note 16: 50% on the value of the steel content, on top of the aluminum duty already charged on its aluminum content. Ended April 6, 2026.

changes.title: Country reciprocal rates replace the 10% baseline
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 set country rates for goods entered from August 7, 2025: Indonesia, Cambodia, Thailand, Malaysia and the Philippines +19%, Vietnam, Taiwan and Bangladesh +20%, India +25%, the UK +10%. EU goods with a column 1 rate under 15% paid 15% in total (9903.02.20) — so a Free German toy paid 15%. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Extra 40% on products of Brazil
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 added 40% on Brazilian goods, on top of the 10% reciprocal duty: 50% in all on Brazilian toys and sports goods. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Law ends the de minimis exemption from July 1, 2027
changes.detail: Section 70531 of P.L. 119-21 terminates the de minimis exemption of 19 U.S.C. 1321(a)(2)(C) effective July 1, 2027, as CBP's 2026 rules note.

changes.title: Section 232 doubled to 50% on the metal content
changes.detail: Proclamation 10947 raised the aluminum and steel duties from 25% to 50% (UK stayed at 25%). For the 22 Chapter 95 aluminum derivative lines it applied to the value of the aluminum content. Ended April 5, 2026.

changes.title: China reciprocal duty cut from 125% to 10%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14298 cut the reciprocal duty on Chinese goods to 10% for goods entered from May 14, 2025. Chinese toys and consoles then paid 30% (10% + 20% fentanyl) until November 9, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China reciprocal duty raised to 125%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14266 raised the reciprocal duty on Chinese goods to 125% from April 10, 2025, and paused the higher country rates announced on April 2 for other countries (Vietnam 46%, Cambodia 49%, Indonesia 32%), which never took effect. With the 20% fentanyl duty, Chinese toys and consoles paid 145% until May 13, 2025, and List 4A sports goods 152.5% plus the base rate.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) from April 5, 2025, and country rates (9903.02.xx); Canada and Mexico excluded. No Chapter 95 product was exempt. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Section 232 aluminum duty reaches 22 sports and fishing lines
changes.detail: Proclamation 10895 extended the aluminum duty to the derivative articles Commerce listed (90 FR 11251), including 22 Chapter 95 lines: snowboards (9506.11.40.80), tennis-racket frames and parts (9506.51.40, .60), badminton rackets (9506.59.40.40), roller skates (9506.70.20.90), exercise equipment (9506.91), archery (9506.99.05), baseball, football, hockey and lacrosse equipment, swimming pools, other sports goods (9506.99.60.80), fishing reels and parts (9507.30) and landing nets (9507.90.60). From all countries: 25% on the value of the aluminum content (9903.85.08), 50% from June 4, 2025, ended April 6, 2026. Products of Russia or made with Russian aluminum: 200% (9903.85.68), still in force.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty raised to 20%
changes.detail: The IEEPA duty on products of China and Hong Kong (9903.01.20, then 9903.01.24) went from +10% (from February 4, 2025) to +20%, the first extra duty on Chinese toys since List 4B was suspended in 2019. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01); USMCA-qualifying goods exempt from March 7, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10), later raised to +35%; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt from March 7, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: ASTM F963-23 becomes the mandatory U.S. toy standard
changes.detail: CPSC's direct final rule made ASTM F963-23 the toy safety standard of 16 CFR part 1250 (section 106 of the CPSIA). Toys for children 12 and under must be third-party tested to it by a CPSC-accepted laboratory and certified on a Children's Product Certificate.

changes.title: China List 4A duty cut to 7.5%
changes.detail: Under the Phase One agreement USTR cut the List 4A duty (9903.88.15) from 15% to 7.5%. The rate on the 81 Chapter 95 lines has been 7.5% ever since.

changes.title: China List 4B — toys and consoles — suspended before it took effect
changes.detail: USTR suspended indefinitely the 15% List 4B duty (9903.88.16) that was to start December 15, 2019. List 4B held 28 Chapter 95 subheadings — toys, video game consoles, playing cards, board games, most Christmas decorations, artificial Christmas trees, festive articles, rackets, roller skates, fishing rods and cheaper reels — so those Chinese goods never paid a China Section 301 list duty.

changes.title: China Section 301 List 4A reaches sports goods
changes.detail: The fourth China Section 301 list put +15% on 57 Chapter 95 subheadings: billiard and bowling equipment, coin-operated games, glass Christmas ornaments, most sports and exercise equipment, fish hooks, lures and reels over $8.45, and amusement rides. understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of toys, games and sports equipment were **$37.02B in 2025**, 14.7% less than the $43.41B of 2024 and well below the $55.20B peak of 2022. Toys, dolls and puzzles (heading 9503) were the largest group at $14.68B (40%), followed by video game consoles, card, board and arcade games (9504, $9.22B, of which consoles $6.73B), sports and exercise equipment (9506, $7.49B) and Christmas and festive articles (9505, $4.33B).

The supplier map moved fast in 2025. **China** fell 37.0% to $20.19B, from $32.04B in 2024, in a year when Chinese goods paid IEEPA duties of up to 145% (April–May 2025), but still shipped $9.77B of toys and $3.34B of the $4.33B of Christmas and festive articles. **Vietnam** rose 140.1% to $7.13B and became the largest supplier of heading 9504 ($4.04B of consoles, card and other games) and the second for toys ($1.95B). **Mexico** ($1.96B, +12.3%) ships mostly toys; **Taiwan** ($1.33B) mostly exercise and other sports equipment; **Japan** ($873M, +59.3%) mostly heading 9504 games and consoles. Indonesia ($724M), Cambodia ($685M, +81.2%), Thailand ($658M) and Malaysia ($456M) all grew. Canada supplied $400M, mostly sports equipment.

The figures are annual and stop at 2025, before the 2026 tariff changes (the end of the IEEPA duties in February, the Section 301 tariffs from July 24, 2026 and the Canada Section 338 duty from August 22); they do not show what those changes did. Duty-collected figures are not available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
Most Chapter 95 goods have **no base duty**, so the tariff a shipment pays **depends almost entirely on where it comes from**. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — taken from the current tariff schedule.

Since the IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026, the extra duty is mainly the **Section 301 tariff on 60 economies** that started July 24, 2026: **+12.5% for China, Vietnam and Thailand**, **+10% for Indonesia, Cambodia, India and Malaysia**, and **10% in total for Taiwan and the EU, 12.5% for Japan and South Korea** — which on a Free toy is the whole duty. **China adds 7.5% more on the 81 List 4A lines** (mostly sports goods), but not on toys or consoles. **Brazil** pays +37.5%. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico pay nothing; from **Canada**, toys, video game consoles, hockey equipment, exercise equipment and the other goods on 27 listed lines owe the **50% Section 338 duty** whatever is claimed.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 95: Toys, Games & Sports Equipment — Import Rules & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Toys into the U.S.: CPSC Toy Rules, Children's Product Certificate, eFiling & Tariff Engineering (HTS Ch. 95) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What toys, games and sporting goods need at U.S. entry — ASTM F963-23 (16 CFR 1250), small-parts and lead rules, third-party testing, the Children's Product Certificate and CPSC eFiling since July 8, 2026, FCC rules for consoles, the excise tax on fishing tackle — and the legal ways to pay less: origin, USMCA, Chapter 98, first sale, drawback, FTZ and rulings.

tariffEngineering.intro:
Toys need no import license, but they carry **more safety paperwork than almost any other consumer good**. A toy for children 12 or younger must meet the mandatory toy standard (**ASTM F963-23**, 16 CFR part 1250), the small-parts, lead and phthalate limits, be **tested by a CPSC-accepted laboratory**, carry tracking labels, and be covered by a **Children's Product Certificate** — whose data importers must **eFile with CBP at entry since July 8, 2026**. Consoles and radio-controlled toys need FCC authorization, fishing tackle and archery equipment owe a federal excise tax when sold, and every article must be marked with its country of origin.

On cost, most Chapter 95 lines are Free, so the levers are about the **extra duty**: the **country of origin** (Free outside the 60 Section 301 economies, 10% from Indonesia, Cambodia, India, Malaysia, Taiwan or the EU, 12.5% from China or Vietnam, 50% from Canada on the Section 338 lines), USMCA for Mexican goods, Chapter 98 provisions that the Section 301 duty does not reach, first-sale valuation, drawback and foreign-trade zones. Each lever depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Know the country of origin — it decides almost the whole duty
levers.saves: On a Free toy, the whole duty: 12.5% from China, Vietnam or Thailand, 10% from Indonesia, Cambodia, India, Malaysia, Taiwan or the EU, 12.5% in total from Japan, 50% from Canada on the Section 338 lines, nothing from a country outside the 60 Section 301 economies. On List 4A sports goods China adds 7.5% more.
levers.appliesTo: All lines; the gap is widest on Canadian toys and consoles and on Chinese List 4A sports equipment
levers.document: Production records showing where the article was last substantially transformed — for a toy, typically where it is molded, assembled and decorated, not where it is packed; for goods of Canada or Mexico, the 19 CFR part 102 tariff-shift rules.
levers.caveat: Packing, labeling or adding batteries in a third country does not move the origin. The Section 301 and Section 338 duties follow the country of origin, not the country of export, and CBP can ask for proof.

citations.label: 19 CFR 102.11 (origin of goods of Canada and Mexico)
HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 20, 51, 52

levers.title: Claim USMCA on goods from Mexico — and know its limit for Canada
levers.saves: The 10% Section 301 duty (and the base rate on dutiable sports and fishing lines)
levers.appliesTo: All lines from Mexico; from Canada, every line except the 27 Section 338 lines (toys, consoles, arcade and other game machines, some Christmas and festive articles, golf parts, ice skates, exercise equipment, pools, other sports goods, fishing rods, hockey equipment)
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, kept ready for CBP.
levers.caveat: USMCA does not remove the 50% Section 338 duty on the listed Canadian lines (U.S. note 51(a)). The good must meet its rule of origin in General Note 11. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: HTSUS General Note 11 (USMCA rules of origin)

levers.title: Claim an FTA or AGOA on dutiable sports goods and fishing tackle
levers.saves: The base rate — 2.6% to 9.2%, or 24¢ a reel — on the 48 dutiable lines
levers.appliesTo: Dutiable lines of 9506 and 9507 whose Special column lists the program: AGOA (D, to December 31, 2026), Australia (AU), Korea (KR), Singapore (SG), Chile (CL), CAFTA-DR (P), Japan (JP, on golf clubs, golf parts, tennis rackets not strung, some hooks, reels and line) and the other FTA partners
levers.document: The origin proof each program requires (a certification or declaration of origin, or the AGOA documentation) and records to back it up.
levers.caveat: An FTA removes the base rate but not the 2026 Section 301 duty of a listed country (U.S. note 52(a)) — Japanese and Korean golf clubs still pay 12.5% in total. Toys, games, Christmas articles and amusement rides are Free anyway. GSP (A) has been expired since December 31, 2020.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Use a Chapter 98 provision: adaptive equipment, holiday utilitarian articles, U.S. goods returned
levers.saves: A Chapter 98 entry skips the 2026 Section 301 duty and the Canada Section 338 duty (U.S. notes 51(a), 52(a)): sports and play equipment specially designed or adapted for persons with a permanent disability enters Free (9817.00.96); utilitarian articles in the form of a holiday symbol — light-up figures, plastic or ceramic Christmas tableware — are Free under 9817.95.05; U.S.-made goods returned unchanged pay nothing (9801.00.10).
levers.appliesTo: Adaptive sports equipment; holiday-shaped utilitarian articles classified in plastics, ceramics, glass, textile or lighting headings (not Chapter 95); American toys and sports goods coming back
levers.document: For 9817.00.96, evidence the article is specially designed or adapted for persons with a permanent or chronic disability; for 9817.95.05, a description showing the three-dimensional holiday motif and the underlying subheading; for 9801.00.10, proof of U.S. origin and export.
levers.caveat: 9817.95.01 and 9817.95.05 cover only articles of the subheadings they list (for example 3924.10, 3926.90, 6307.90, 6911.10, 6912.00, 7013, 9405.21–9405.50), not Christmas ornaments or decorations of heading 9505, which are Free anyway. Under 9802.00.80 (U.S. components assembled abroad) the Section 301 duty still applies to the value added abroad.

provisions.text: Articles specially designed or adapted for the use or benefit of physically or mentally handicapped persons (other than articles for the blind)
Utilitarian articles in the form of a three-dimensional representation of a symbol or motif clearly associated with a specific holiday in the United States
Products of the United States returned without having been advanced in value or improved

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 51(a), 52(a)

levers.title: Check the heading: toy, sports article, festive article or something else
levers.saves: The gap between a Free Chapter 95 line and a dutiable one elsewhere — and between Chapter 95 lines: soccer balls and footballs are Free, basketballs and volleyballs 4.8%; golf balls Free, golf clubs 4.4%; fishing reels 9.2% up to $2.70 each, 24¢ each to $8.45, 3.9% above. For Chinese goods it also decides List 4A (+7.5%) or the suspended List 4B.
levers.appliesTo: Toys sold with other items (note 4), pet toys (note 5, excluded), drones (8806), children's bicycles (8712), Christmas lighting strings (9405), sports bags (4202) and apparel (chapters 61–62), trading cards, pickleball sets
levers.document: A product description, photos and the retail packaging; for a set, what each item is and why the toy gives the essential character.
levers.caveat: Classification follows the HTS notes and CBP rulings, not marketing. CBP classifies Pokémon trading cards as playing cards (9504.40, NY N359352) and a pickleball set under 9506.99.60 (NY N347450); a ruling on a similar article is guidance, not a ruling for yours.

citations.label: HTSUS Chapter 95, notes 1, 3, 4, 5 and subheading note 1

levers.title: Value at the first sale for export when you buy through a middleman
levers.saves: Every ad valorem duty is charged on a lower value — the 10%–12.5% Section 301 duty, List 4A and Section 338 included — when the factory price to a trading company or licensor is lower than the price you pay. For fishing reels the value per reel also decides the rate bracket.
levers.appliesTo: All lines bought through a trading company, agent-buyer or brand owner rather than straight from the factory
levers.document: Proof that the first sale was a bona fide sale for export to the United States at arm's length: the factory invoice, contracts and payment records.
levers.caveat: Only a sale clearly destined for the U.S. qualifies, and the importer must be able to show the earlier price at entry.

levers.title: Recover duty on goods you export or destroy
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid, when imported toys, consoles or sports goods are exported (for example to Canadian or Latin American stores) or destroyed under CBP supervision
levers.appliesTo: Any line that paid a duty
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import and export (or destruction) records that tie the goods together.
levers.caveat: Claims have filing deadlines and record-keeping rules; check whether a given Chapter 99 duty is eligible before relying on it.

levers.title: Hold, kit or relabel goods in a foreign-trade zone
levers.saves: No duty on goods re-exported from the zone, and duty deferred until they leave it for the U.S. market — useful for seasonal toy and Christmas inventory
levers.appliesTo: Any line — useful for distribution centers that also ship to Canada and Mexico
levers.document: Zone admission (CBP Form 214) and the zone operator's inventory records.
levers.caveat: Goods entered for consumption from a zone pay the duties in force on the entry date. CPSC certificate eFiling for goods entered from a zone starts January 8, 2027.

levers.title: Claim back IEEPA duties paid in 2025–2026
levers.saves: The IEEPA duties paid on goods entered between February 2025 and February 23, 2026 — for example 145%, then 30% and 20% on Chinese toys and consoles, 20% on Vietnamese and 19% on Indonesian or Malaysian goods — with interest
levers.appliesTo: Past entries of any line that paid an IEEPA duty (9903.01.xx, 9903.02.xx)
levers.document: A CAPE Declaration filed in the ACE Portal by the importer of record or its customs broker, listing the entries, plus ACH refund details on file.
levers.caveat: Phase 1 covers unliquidated entries and entries within the voluntary reliquidation period; other entries may need a protest or court action. It does not refund Section 301, List 4A or Section 338 duties. Refunds go to the importer of record.

levers.title: Get a binding classification ruling
levers.saves: Certainty where the line decides the rate or the extra duty: toy or not, set or not, List 4A or 4B line, Section 338 line or not, Chapter 95 or a utilitarian heading
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the design, use or materials decide the line
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the article, with photos, a sample and the retail packaging.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the article described; a changed design or packaging may need a new one.

rules.title: Toys must meet ASTM F963-23, the mandatory toy safety standard, plus the added water-bead (from March 12, 2026) and neck-float (from June 15, 2026) requirements

Toys for children under 3 may not have small parts that fit the test cylinder; toys and games with small parts for ages 3 to 6, latex balloons, and small balls and marbles for children 3 and older need the choking-hazard warning on the package

Children's products: lead content up to 100 ppm in any accessible part and 90 ppm in paint and coatings; toys and child-care articles: no more than 0.1% of each of eight phthalates (DEHP, DBP, BBP, DINP, DIBP, DPENP, DHEXP, DCHP) in plasticized parts

Children's products must be third-party tested by a CPSC-accepted laboratory, carry permanent tracking labels, and be covered by a Children's Product Certificate; since July 8, 2026 the importer must eFile the certificate data in ACE with the entry (mail shipments: in CPSC's Product Registry before arrival; FTZ entries from January 8, 2027)

Radio-frequency devices — game consoles and handhelds with Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, wireless controllers, remote-control toys — may be imported only with a valid FCC equipment authorization or under another import condition

Federal excise tax on the importer's first sale: sport fishing equipment 10% (fishing rods and poles capped at $10, tackle boxes 3%); bows of 30 lb draw weight or more and archery parts, quivers and broadheads 11%; arrow shafts a per-shaft tax
Country-of-origin marking in English, legible, indelible and permanent enough to reach the ultimate purchaser — on the article or, where an exception applies, on its retail package
Report the Chapter 99 headings with the line: the 2026 Section 301 heading for the country, China List 4A (9903.88.15), Brazil (9903.05.01), Canada Section 338 (9903.03.12 / 9903.03.14)

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 20, 50–52

groups.label: Toys, dolls, puzzles, building sets, scale models, tricycles and toy scooters
groups.note: Every toy for a child 12 or under is a children's product: ASTM F963-23, small parts (under 3), lead and phthalates, third-party testing and a CPC eFiled at entry. The statistical suffix follows the youngest age on the label. From Canada, 50% Section 338 even under USMCA.

groups.label: Video game consoles, board and card games, billiards, arcade, casino and bowling equipment
groups.note: Consoles and controllers with radios need FCC authorization. Board games, cards and handheld games meant for children 12 or under are children's products under the CPSC rules. 9504.30, 9504.50 and 9504.90.40 from Canada owe the 50% Section 338 duty.

groups.label: Christmas ornaments, artificial Christmas trees, Halloween and party articles, magic tricks
groups.note: Christmas decorations are general-use products unless designed for children; Christmas lighting strings are 9405, not this chapter. Glass ornaments are on China's List 4A, the rest of 9505 on suspended List 4B.

groups.label: Sports and exercise equipment: golf, balls, skis, skates, fitness machines, pools, archery, hockey
groups.note: Sports equipment designed for children 12 or under is a children's product. Bows and archery parts owe the 11% excise tax. Most lines are on China's List 4A; exercise equipment, pools, ice skates, golf parts and hockey gear from Canada owe the Section 338 duty.

groups.label: Fishing rods, reels, hooks, line, lures and other fishing tackle; landing nets
groups.note: All lines are dutiable (3.7%–9.2% or 24¢ a reel). The importer owes the 10% sport-fishing excise tax when it sells rods, reels, lures, line and other tackle.

groups.label: Amusement park rides, carousels, water park and fairground amusements, traveling circuses and theaters
groups.note: Amusement rides are Free; China List 4A adds 7.5% to the 12.5% Section 301 duty.

Toys were on China's Section 301 List 4B, which USTR suspended in December 2019, so the 7.5% List 4A duty does not apply. The IEEPA duties that raised Chinese toys to 145% in April–May 2025, then 30% and 20%, ended February 24, 2026. Chinese sports goods on List 4A pay 20% plus their base rate.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on toys from Canada?
searchedAs: tariffs on toys from canada to us
are there tariffs on toys from canada
faqs.answer: Yes. Since August 22, 2026 products of Canada classified in 9503.00.00 — all toys — pay a 50% Section 338 duty (9903.03.14), and U.S. note 51(a) applies it even when USMCA is claimed. Non-qualifying Canadian toys also pay the 10% Section 301 duty: 60%. The same 50% reaches Canadian video game consoles, arcade games, hockey equipment, exercise equipment and pools.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on toys, games and trading cards from Japan?
searchedAs: tariffs on trading cards from japan
faqs.answer: 12.5% in total (9903.05.49): Japanese goods pay 12.5% where the base rate is lower, and every Chapter 95 line is Free or under 10%. That covers toys, video game consoles, trading cards and golf clubs — even those the U.S.–Japan Trade Agreement makes Free. From August 2025 to February 23, 2026 the IEEPA rate was 15% in total.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on video game consoles?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on video game consoles
faqs.answer: Video game consoles, handheld game machines and controllers (9504.50.00) are Free, so they pay only the extra duty for their origin: 12.5% from China or Vietnam (consoles were on suspended List 4B), 10% from Malaysia or Indonesia, 12.5% in total from Japan. From Canada they pay 50% under Section 338, even with a USMCA claim.

faqs.question: What is the HTS code for video game consoles and controllers?
searchedAs: video game console hs tariff code
faqs.answer: 9504.50.00.00: video game consoles that display on a TV, monitor or other external screen, video game machines with their own screen, and their parts and accessories such as controllers. Coin-, card- or token-operated arcade machines are 9504.30; other game machines not operated by payment 9504.90.40. All are Free.

faqs.question: What is the HTS code for toys?
faqs.answer: Toys are 9503.00.00 (Free) — dolls, plush toys, building sets, puzzles, ride-on toys, scale models and their parts. The statistical suffix depends on the product and the youngest age on the label: inflatable toy balls and balloons .11 (under 3) or .13 (3–12); other toys .71 (under 3) or .73 (3–12); .90 for articles that are not children's products. Pet toys, children's bicycles (8712) and drones (8806) are not in 9503.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for board games, puzzles and dolls?
searchedAs: hs code for toys and games
faqs.answer: Board games such as chess, checkers, backgammon and other games played on a special board, plus dominoes, poker chips and dice, are 9504.90.60. Jigsaw and other puzzles and dolls are toys of 9503.00.00. Both are Free; the extra duty depends on the origin.

faqs.question: What is the tariff code for trading cards and playing cards?
faqs.answer: Playing cards are 9504.40.00 (Free), and CBP classified Pokémon trading cards from Japan there (NY N359352, March 2026). From Japan they pay 12.5% in total, from China 12.5%, from the EU 10%.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on Christmas decorations and artificial Christmas trees?
faqs.answer: Christmas ornaments, nativity scenes, artificial trees and other Christmas decorations (9505.10) are Free. From China they pay 12.5% — except glass ornaments (9505.10.10), which are on List 4A and pay 20%. Artificial trees of plastics are 9505.10.40.10. Christmas lights are not in Chapter 95 (heading 9405).

faqs.question: What are the tariffs on sporting goods, golf clubs and exercise equipment?
faqs.answer: Sports equipment is heading 9506: golf clubs 9506.31 (4.4%), golf balls 9506.32 (Free), exercise equipment 9506.91 (4.6%), basketballs 9506.62.80 (4.8%); CBP put a pickleball set in 9506.99.60 (4%). Chinese golf clubs pay 24.4% and treadmills 24.6% (List 4A), Vietnamese 16.9% and 17.1%, Taiwanese 10%. The Section 232 metals duty on exercise equipment ended April 6, 2026.

faqs.question: What are the tariffs on fishing rods, reels and tackle?
faqs.answer: Fishing rods are 9507.10 (6%), reels 9507.30 (9.2% up to $2.70, 24¢ each to $8.45, 3.9% above), artificial lures and flies 9507.90.70 (9%), hooks 9507.20 (4%–4.8%). Chinese rods pay 18.5%, lures 29% (List 4A). The importer also owes a 10% federal excise tax on its sale of sport fishing equipment (rods capped at $10).

faqs.question: Can importers get the 2025 toy tariffs refunded?
faqs.answer: The IEEPA duties, yes. After the Supreme Court ruled on February 20, 2026 that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, CBP opened CAPE in ACE: the importer of record or its broker files a CAPE Declaration listing the entries, and CBP refunds the IEEPA duties with interest. Section 301, List 4A and Section 338 duties are not refunded, and refunds go to the importer, not to retail buyers.

faqs.question: What does a toy importer need: Children's Product Certificate, ASTM F963 and CPSC eFiling?
faqs.answer: Toys for children 12 or under must meet ASTM F963-23 (16 CFR part 1250) and the small-parts, lead and phthalate rules, be tested by a CPSC-accepted laboratory, carry tracking labels, and be covered by a Children's Product Certificate. Since July 8, 2026 the importer must eFile the certificate data in ACE with the entry; for mail shipments, in CPSC's Product Registry before arrival.
